newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Oil up in defiance of looming Iraq exports.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil up in defiance of looming Iraq exports.

text.p: World oil prices firmed on Thursday as demand for gasoline in the United States more than offset bearish news about Iraqi oil sales.
Brent crude oil, the world benchmark grade, closed up 38 cents at $18.68 a barrel on the London futures market.
Prices have fallen about 26 percent from almost $25 earlier this year and recently scrambled up from a 13-month low of $17.32 a barrel.
U.S. government figures released on Wednesday showed falls in gasoline stocks of nearly four million barrels last week.
This helped keep a floor under gasoline prices on the east coast of the United States which gained more than $2 a barrel in recent weeks.
Asian demand for naphtha, a petrochemical feedstock, has also snapped higher in recent days and there are other "hot spots" of oil products demand.
Adding a twist to the crude supply picture is a possible hiccup in the Gulf of Mexico and a delay to a resumption of output in Colombia.
Crews were evacuated from several offshore rigs on Wednesday as a strengthening tropical depression threatened one of the most productive oil and gas regions in the Gulf of Mexico.
And in Colombia Occidental aims to resume output from its Cano Limon oil field which has been paralysed for a week after leftist rebels attacked pipelines and pumps.
But the company fears damage to the oil wells could prevent or delay their efforts.

Meanwhile, Iraq is expected to more than double its oil exports next month to around 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd) to make up for a gap between the end of the first "oil-for-food" deal and the beginning of the second.

The second deal began on June 8 but Iraq has delayed exporting oil for two months and will now have to sell oil at a much higher rate in August than previously reckoned, or forego some of its oil sales under the scheme.
The United Nations confirmed late on Wednesday that Iraq must sell around $1 billion worth of oil by early September under the renewed "oil-for-food" deal.

"According to the resolution, Iraq will have to sell the $1 billion authorised in whatever is remaining of the 90-day period," said the U.N. Secretary-General's spokesperson on Iraq, Myriam Desabbles.

The "oil-for-food" deal covers two consecutive 90-day periods allowing $1 billion worth of oil sales in each period. But "there is a leeway of no more than five percent" that can be carried over to the second period, Desabbles said.
"Iraq is a bearish cloud on the horizon," said Charles Gray at brokers Prudential Bache in London.
"If they want their full entitlement of food and medicine they will have to pump the oil," he added.
In addition to Iraqi barrels, Germany is planning to begin selling some of its strategic oil stocks in August.
Also, crude oil supply from the North Sea is likely to stay unexpectedly strong.
August loading programmes at 4.45 million bpd are little changed from July after a survey of field operators had earlier suggested a drop of 245,000 bpd in August.
